opus-5.5.text:
I think memory is one of the most underexplored pieces of the puzzle right now. If you look at how we train these models, there's this very sharp divide: you have a huge, expensive pre-training phase where the weights absorb everything, and then at inference time the model is essentially frozen. Whatever it learns in a conversation lives in the context window, and when that conversation ends, it's gone. That's a strange way for an intelligent system to work. Humans don't operate like that. We're constantly consolidating experience, deciding what's worth keeping, and building on it over years.

So long-term memory, to me, is really about closing that loop between training and inference, letting a system accumulate knowledge continuously rather than in these big discrete jumps. And I don't think the answer is simply making the context window longer and longer. That helps, and it's been impressive to see, but stuffing a million tokens into attention isn't the same as having a structured memory that you can selectively write to, retrieve from, and reorganize. There's something about the act of deciding what to remember, and compressing it, that I suspect is tied up with actual understanding.

The shared part is where it gets really interesting for me. One of the themes I keep coming back to, especially with the nature-inspired work we do at Sakana, is collective intelligence. Individual organisms aren't that smart on their own, but populations, colonies and cultures accumulate knowledge across individuals and across generations. Human civilization is basically a shared memory system. We write things down, we teach each other, and no single person has to rediscover everything from scratch.

If you imagine many AI agents that can deposit what they've learned into some common store, and others can draw on that, refine it, argue with it even, you start to get something that looks less like one giant monolithic model and more like an ecosystem that improves over time. That feels to me like a more natural and probably more robust path than just scaling up a single network. It also opens the door to more open-ended processes, where the system keeps generating new stepping stones rather than converging on one answer.

Of course there are hard problems: what gets written, how you prevent errors propagating through the shared store, how you handle forgetting. But I'd much rather be working on those questions than squeezing another half percent out of a benchmark with the same architecture we've had since 2017.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, actually, because it's one of the things that feels most obviously missing from current systems. Right now, every time you start a conversation with one of these models, it's basically waking up with amnesia. It has this enormous amount of knowledge baked into the weights, but it has no idea who you are, what you talked about yesterday, what it got wrong last week. And we've been papering over that with context windows, which is sort of a brute force approach. You just stuff more and more into the prompt and hope the attention mechanism sorts it out.

And I'll be honest, I have mixed feelings about that, because I was involved in creating that mechanism, and I don't think it was ever really designed to be a memory system. Attention is great at relating things within a sequence, but memory is a different problem. Memory is about deciding what's worth keeping, compressing it, retrieving it when it's relevant, and, crucially, forgetting the stuff that isn't. Humans are very good at forgetting, and I think we underrate how important that is.

So when I think about long-term memory, I'm less interested in just making the context bigger and more interested in systems that actually learn from their experience in a persistent way. The thing that really excites me is this idea of models that keep updating, where interacting with the world actually changes them, rather than everything being frozen at training time and then you just do inference forever.

The shared memory piece is maybe the more radical one. If you have lots of agents, or lots of instances of a model, and they can pool what they've learned, then you get something that doesn't look like an individual intelligence anymore. It looks more like a culture, or a civilisation. One agent figures something out and everyone else immediately benefits. That's a kind of collective learning that humans do very slowly through language and books, and these systems could potentially do it almost instantly.

Now, there are obvious risks there. If one of them picks up a bad habit or a wrong belief, that can propagate just as fast. And there are real questions around privacy, around whose memories are being shared and who consented to that. But I think architecturally it's where things are heading. The current paradigm of giant static models that we retrain every few months feels like a transitional phase to me. I think in ten years we'll look back and find it a bit strange that we had these incredibly capable systems that couldn't remember anything.

astra-6.text:
I think memory is going to be a really important part of this. At the moment, you can have a useful conversation with a model, but you’re often having to supply the context again the next time. If a system is going to work with you over a long period, it needs some way of retaining what you’ve done together and bringing back the relevant parts.

The interesting question is what it should remember. Keeping everything isn’t necessarily useful. You need to decide what matters, when to retrieve it, and when something is out of date. A memory shouldn’t become a fact that the system can never reconsider.

Shared memory adds another dimension: could one system learn something useful and make that available to others without each of them repeating the same work? That sounds powerful, but you also need to preserve where the information came from and how reliable it is. Otherwise, you can end up sharing mistakes very efficiently.

So I think there’s a lot of potential there. But the important capability isn’t just storage—it’s being able to use past experience appropriately.

sol-6.1.text:
I think memory is going to be a really important part of it. At the moment, you can have a useful conversation with a model, but so much of what it learns about what you’re doing disappears when that conversation ends. You’d like a system that can build on previous interactions without having to be told everything again.

Shared memory adds another interesting dimension. If several agents are working on a problem, they could contribute to a common store of knowledge rather than each having to rediscover the same things. But then you have to decide what deserves to be remembered, how to correct it, and how to handle conflicting information. You don’t want one agent’s mistake becoming something every other agent treats as fact.

So I think the interesting question is more than just how much information we can store. It’s how a system learns to retrieve the right information, update it, and sometimes forget it. That seems like a substantial part of making these systems useful over longer periods of time.
